Name: Karnak Temple Complex
Build_by: Senusret I, Hatshepsut, Thutmose III, Amenhotep III, Seti I, Ramesses II, and Ptolemaic rulers
Description: The largest religious sanctuary in ancient Egypt, primarily dedicated to the Theban Triad of Amun-Ra, Mut, and Khonsu. It is renowned for the Great Hypostyle Hall containing 134 colossal sandstone papyrus columns, sacred lakes, massive pylons, and towering obelisks.
age: Approximately 4,000 years old (Middle Kingdom through Roman Period)
Offerings: Conical loaves of emmer wheat bread
Jars of date wine and barley beer
Fine linen textiles and gold tableware
Offerings_status: Unverified. No sources; several items look illustrative rather than recorded.

Name: Luxor Temple
Location: East Bank of the Nile, Luxor, Egypt
Build_by: Amenhotep III and Ramesses II (with additions by Tutankhamun, Horemheb, and Alexander the Great)
Description: A grand riverside temple dedicated to the rejuvenation of kingship rather than a specific deity cult, serving as the central setting for the annual Opet Festival. It was linked directly to Karnak via the 2.7-kilometer Avenue of Sphinxes.
age: Approximately 3,420 years old (New Kingdom, 18th to 19th Dynasties)
Offerings: White bread cones and honey cakes
Offerings_status: Unverified. No sources; several items look illustrative rather than recorded.
Audit_notes: The kingship reading is a scholarly interpretation. Gods added because the temple also served Amun, Mut and Khonsu.

Name: Great Temple of Abu Simbel
Build_by: Ramesses II
Description: A massive rock-cut cliff temple fronted by four colossal 20-meter seated statues of Ramesses II. Dedicated to Ra-Horakhty, Ptah, Amun, and the deified Ramesses himself, it was engineered so the rising sun lights three of the four sanctuary statues twice a year, while Ptah stays in shadow.
Offerings_status: Unverified. No sources; several items look illustrative rather than recorded.
Audit_notes: Corrected: the sun lights three of the four sanctuary statues, and Ptah stays dark.
Ra-Horakhty is linked to Ra. The fourth dedication is the deified Ramesses II.

Name: Mortuary Temple of Hatshepsut (Djeser-Djeseru)
Location: Deir el-Bahari, West Bank of Luxor, Egypt
Build_by: Pharaoh Hatshepsut (designed by royal architect Senenmut)
Description: A masterpiece of ancient classical architecture rising in three stepped colonnaded terraces set against the towering cliffs of Deir el-Bahari. Built to honor Amun and perpetuate Hatshepsut's royal cult, it features painted reliefs of the historic expedition to the Land of Punt.
Offerings: Living myrrh and frankincense trees from Punt
Ebony wood and elephant ivory tusks
Sweet grape wine and clear spring water
Barley loaves baked in conical pots
Offerings_status: Unverified. No sources; several items look illustrative rather than recorded.
Audit_notes: Build dates are her reign; the temple itself took a shorter part of it.

Name: Temple of Edfu (Temple of Horus)
Build_by: Ptolemy III Euergetes through Ptolemy XII Auletes
Description: The most intact and best-preserved temple in Egypt, dedicated to the falcon god Horus of Behdet. It preserves complete roofed halls, intricate mythological inscriptions recounting the cosmic battle between Horus and Set, and an intact granite naos shrine.
Offerings: Wine jars sealed with mud caps
Green and black eye kohl pigments
Bundles of fresh papyrus and lotus stems
Offerings_status: Unverified. No sources; several items look illustrative rather than recorded.

Name: Temple of Philae (Temple of Isis)
Location: Agilkia Island (originally Philae Island), Aswan, Egypt
Build_by: Nectanebo I, Ptolemy II Philadelphus, and Roman Emperors Augustus and Trajan
Description: An island sanctuary dedicated to the mother goddess Isis, renowned as one of the last operating pagan temples in the Mediterranean basin. It preserves the final recorded Egyptian hieroglyphic inscription, carved on August 24, 394 CE.
age: Approximately 2,400 years old (30th Dynasty through Roman Period)
Offerings: Daily libations at the 365 offering tables of the Abaton on Bigeh
Freshly picked lotus buds and water lilies
Fine white linen robes for the cult statue
Offerings_status: Unverified. No sources; several items look illustrative rather than recorded.
Audit_notes: Corrected offering: the 365 offering tables belong to the Abaton on Bigeh, the island beside Philae, and the number comes from one secondary source.

Name: Temple of Kom Ombo
Build_by: Ptolemy VI Philometor with additions by later Ptolemies and Romans
Description: A unique double temple featuring identical symmetrical courts, hypostyle halls, and twin sanctuaries along a central axis. The northern half honored the falcon god Haroeris (Horus the Elder) while the southern half honored Sobek, the crocodile deity of fertility.
age: Approximately 2,200 years old (Ptolemaic to Roman Period)
Offerings: Fresh river fish and marsh birds
Jars of thick dark date beer
Spelt loaves and sesame seed cakes
Offerings_status: Unverified. No sources; several items look illustrative rather than recorded.
Audit_notes: Haroeris is linked to Horus, since he is the elder form.

Name: Dendera Temple Complex (Temple of Hathor)
Build_by: Ptolemy XII Auletes, Cleopatra VII Philopator, Augustus, and Tiberius
Description: One of Egypt's most intact sacred complexes, dedicated to Hathor, goddess of love, joy, and music. Famous for its vibrant celestial ceiling reliefs, massive Hathoric column capitals, subterranean crypts, and the original chamber of the Dendera Zodiac.
age: Approximately 2,080 years old (Late Ptolemaic to Early Roman Period)
Offerings: Sweet unfermented grape must and date wine
Offerings_status: Unverified. No sources; several items look illustrative rather than recorded.

Name: Temple of Seti I at Abydos
Build_by: Pharaoh Seti I (completed by his son Ramesses II)
Description: An L-shaped limestone mortuary temple built upon the sacred cult center of Osiris, recognized for having the finest, most delicate raised reliefs of the New Kingdom. It houses seven distinct vaulted chapels and the famous Abydos King List containing 76 royal cartouches.
Offerings: White emmer loaves and sesame rolls
Sacrificial bull meat and gazelle haunches
Clear well water from the Osireion
Incense grains burned in bronze arms
Linen strips for the Osirian mysteries
Offerings_status: Unverified. No sources; several items look illustrative rather than recorded.
Audit_notes: Often called a memorial temple rather than a mortuary temple. Not checked against a source.
Gods added from its seven chapels, not from the source file. Not checked against a source.

Name: The Ramesseum
Location: West Bank of Luxor (Theban Necropolis), Egypt
Build_by: Ramesses II
Description: The sprawling mortuary temple of Ramesses II, designed to perpetuate his divine cult and celebrate the glory of his reign. It contains vast mudbrick granaries, reliefs of the Battle of Kadesh, and the fragments of an enormous 1,000-ton fallen granite colossus.
Offerings: Roasted whole bulls and young calves
Aromatic oils in carved calcite vessels
Offerings_status: Unverified. No sources; several items look illustrative rather than recorded.
Audit_notes: Build dates are his whole reign. Amun is added from general knowledge, not checked against a source.

Name: Medinet Habu (Mortuary Temple of Ramesses III)
Location: West Bank of Luxor (Theban Necropolis), Egypt
Build_by: Ramesses III
Description: A fortress-like mortuary temple enclosed within massive fortified mudbrick walls and a Syrian-style migdol gateway. Its deeply carved pylon walls preserve crucial historical records depicting the defense of Egypt against the Sea Peoples and Libyan coalitions.
Offerings: Heaps of threshed barley and emmer wheat
Linen garments dyed with indigo and red
Censer bowls of burning aromatic gums
Sweet dried raisins and pressed dates
Offerings_status: Unverified. No sources; several items look illustrative rather than recorded.
Audit_notes: Amun is added from general knowledge, not checked against a source.

Name: Valley Temple of Khafre
Build_by: Pharaoh Khafre
Description: An Old Kingdom architectural marvel built from massive cyclopean limestone blocks cased in polished red Aswan granite, floored with translucent white calcite alabaster. It stood next to the Great Sphinx and may have been a setting for royal funerary rites; whether these included the Opening of the Mouth or mummification is debated.
Offerings: Purification libations of sweet well water
The seven sacred canonical funerary oils
Beer poured into red clay conical cups
Offerings_status: Unverified. No sources; several items look illustrative rather than recorded.
Audit_notes: Corrected: its role in mummification and Opening of the Mouth rites is debated, not settled.
No god link: this is a royal funerary temple.

Name: Temple of Esna (Temple of Khnum)
Build_by: Ptolemy VI Philometor, completed by Roman Emperors Claudius, Vespasian, and Decius
Description: Excavated from beneath nine meters of modern city deposits, this preserved hypostyle hall rests on 24 sandstone columns, each crowned with unique floral and palm capitals. Dedicated to the ram-headed potter god Khnum, it features intricate astronomical ceiling murals.
age: Approximately 2,100 years old (Ptolemaic through Roman Period)
Offerings: Jars of fresh cool Nile water
Barley mash and leavened bread loaves
Woven garments honoring the goddess Neith
Offerings_status: Unverified. No sources; several items look illustrative rather than recorded.
Audit_notes: Neith is added because the offerings field names her.

Name: Temple of Kalabsha
Location: New Kalabsha Island, Aswan Governorate, Egypt
Build_by: Roman Emperor Augustus (over an earlier 18th Dynasty foundation by Amenhotep II)
Description: The largest free-standing sandstone temple in Lower Nubia, dedicated to Mandulis, the Nubian solar deity, along with Isis and Osiris. Rescued during the UNESCO Nubia Campaign, the entire temple was dismantled and relocated to save it from the waters of Lake Nasser.
Offerings: Nubian alluvial gold dust and nuggets
Slain desert game and fattened cattle
Sweet milk poured into stone basins
Imported Roman amphorae of red wine
Offerings_status: Unverified. No sources; several items look illustrative rather than recorded.
Audit_notes: Amenhotep II built an earlier foundation, not this temple.

Name: Mortuary Temple of Amenhotep III (Kom el-Hettan)
Location: West Bank of Luxor (Theban Necropolis), Egypt
Build_by: Pharaoh Amenhotep III
Description: Once the largest and most opulent mortuary temple ever built in Egypt, spanning over 35 hectares and larger than Karnak was at that time, before being dismantled by an ancient earthquake and subsequent quarrying. Its eastern portal is still flanked by the world-famous 18-meter twin Colossi of Memnon.
Offerings: Vessels of hammered gold, silver, and electrum
Raw lapis lazuli and turquoise lumps
Hundreds of fatted bulls presented at royal jubilees
Pure cedar oils and rare ointments
Baskets of fine white bread and pomegranates
Offerings_status: Unverified. No sources; several items look illustrative rather than recorded.
Audit_notes: Corrected: sources agree on about 35 hectares, but only say it exceeded Karnak as Karnak was at that time.
Amun is added from general knowledge, not checked against a source.

Name: Great Temple of Ptah (Hikuptah)
Location: Mit Rahina (Ancient Memphis), Giza Governorate, Egypt
Build_year: c. 1290 BCE – 1213 BCE (western complex; the cult is older)
Build_by: Probably begun by Seti I and developed by Ramesses II
Description: The main sanctuary of Ptah at Memphis, Egypt's ancient capital, and one of the largest temple complexes of its time. Little survives above ground, and the great pylon and hypostyle hall are known mainly from excavation. A colossal statue of Ramesses II stood before the entrance.
age: Approximately 3,300 years old for the surviving western complex (New Kingdom, 19th Dynasty)
Offerings_status: None recorded.
Audit_notes: Added: it fills the gap for Memphis, the old capital, and for Ptah.

Name: Temple of Ra at Heliopolis (Iunu)
Build_year: c. 1950 BCE (the surviving obelisk; the site is older)
Build_by: Senusret I (surviving obelisk), with later work by other kings
Description: The great sanctuary of the sun god at Heliopolis, the centre of Ra and Atum worship. Its buildings were largely quarried away for medieval Cairo. The 21-metre obelisk of Senusret I still stands in place and is generally considered the oldest surviving obelisk.
age: Approximately 3,975 years old for the obelisk (Middle Kingdom, 12th Dynasty)
Offerings_status: None recorded.
Audit_notes: Added: it fills the gap for Heliopolis, the main solar cult centre.

Name: Great Aten Temple (Per-Aten)
Location: Tell el-Amarna (Ancient Akhetaten), Minya Governorate, Egypt
Build_by: Akhenaten
Description: The main temple of Akhenaten's new capital, dedicated to the Aten, the sun disk. Its enclosure measured about 229 by 730 metres, and its courts were open to the sun. It marks the short-lived religious revolution of the Amarna period.
Offerings_status: None recorded.
Audit_notes: Added: it fills the gap for Amarna, and the corpus has 540 documents from the site.

Name: Sun Temple of Nyuserre (Shesepibre)
Build_year: Fifth Dynasty, probably late in the reign of Nyuserre; exact date uncertain
Build_by: Nyuserre Ini
Description: A Fifth Dynasty temple built to honour Ra, with a large open courtyard and a great stone obelisk at its western end. It is the best-known example of the Old Kingdom royal sun temples.
Offerings_status: None recorded.
Audit_notes: Added: it is the main surviving sun temple, and the only Old Kingdom god temple here. The age is approximate, from the Fifth Dynasty date.

Name: Temple of Bastet at Bubastis
Build_year: c. 874 BCE – 343 BCE (the main surviving phases)
Build_by: Osorkon II and Nectanebo II, among others
Description: The main temple of the cat goddess Bastet in the Nile Delta. Herodotus judged it the most beautiful temple he saw in the 5th century BCE. Osorkon II added a festival hall and a granite portal, and Nectanebo II rebuilt the western end.
age: Approximately 2,900 years old for the main surviving phases (Third Intermediate through Late Period)
Offerings_status: None recorded.
Audit_notes: Added: it fills the gap for the Nile Delta and gives Bastet a temple.

Name: Temple of Hibis
Location: Kharga Oasis, New Valley Governorate, Egypt
Build_year: c. 522 BCE – 246 BCE (main building under Darius I, with later additions)
Build_by: Darius I, with additions by Hakor, Nectanebo I, Nectanebo II and Ptolemy II; possibly begun under Psamtik II
Description: A temple to a local form of Amun in Kharga Oasis, and a rare large monument of Persian rule in Egypt. Darius I's cartouches appear in the sanctuary, and later kings extended it.
Offerings_status: None recorded.
Audit_notes: Added: it fills the gap for the Western Desert oases and the Persian period. Whether building began under Psamtik II is disputed, so he is not linked.
